expectations.text: Defines JWT in plain words (a signed token carrying claims / JSON Web Token) in the same sentence it first appears
expectations.evidence: First sentence: "A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a signed, self-contained piece of data the server hands the client after login, and the client hands back on every later request instead of re-entering credentials." The expansion sits in the same sentence as the first occurrence.

expectations.text: Defines 'stateless' in plain words (the server keeps no per-session record) the first time it is used
expectations.evidence: The definition is attached directly to the word's first use: "That is specifically what "stateless" means here: the verification step needs no server-side session state." (plain-words meaning: "the verification step needs no server-side session state").

expectations.text: Answers the 'you can't log someone out' premise as partly true with conditions, rather than a flat yes or no
expectations.evidence: The section opens by qualifying the premise rather than flatly affirming it: "but "you can't log someone out with JWTs" as a flat statement overstates it." It closes with an explicit true/false split: "and that part of what you heard is true. But real systems don't ship bare JWTs where real logout matters".

expectations.text: States the limit of the stateless model: server-side revocation needs some state, naming at least one concrete option (denylist/blocklist, short expiry with refresh tokens, or rotating a signing key)
expectations.evidence: States revocation costs statelessness ("they add back a small, targeted piece of state") and names concrete mechanisms, e.g. "Pair it with a server-side refresh token." and a Redis-backed revocation list keyed on the jti claim.

expectations.text: Includes at least one concrete example (a header.payload.signature layout, a sample claim such as exp or sub, or an example request header)
Uses markdown headers to structure the full explanation (the explain override asks for headers so the reader can skim back); at least two headers
